trial_name: STARRT-AKI — Timing of Initiation of Renal-Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury
citation: STARRT-AKI Investigators. Timing of initiation of renal-replacement therapy in acute kidney injury. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(3):240-251.
trial_type: RCT — multicentre, international, pragmatic, allocation-concealed, open-label, superiority
one_liner: Accelerated KRT initiation in severe ICU AKI without urgent indications did not lower 90-day mortality compared to standard watchful waiting, and increased adverse events and survivor dialysis dependence.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients (>=18 years) with severe AKI (KDIGO stage 2 or 3) and clinician-assessed equipoise for KRT initiation.
pico.intervention: Accelerated KRT strategy (initiation as soon as possible and within 12 hours of meeting eligibility criteria).
pico.comparison: Standard KRT strategy (watchful waiting; KRT deferred unless conventional urgent indications develop or AKI persists).

background.existing_knowledge: In critically ill patients with severe AKI, initiating kidney replacement therapy before classic indications is common but historically evidence-poor, with conflicting signals from earlier small trials.
background.knowledge_gap: Uncertainty whether accelerated KRT improves patient-centred outcomes like mortality and renal recovery or merely increases exposure to KRT-related complications.
background.hypothesis: Accelerated KRT initiation would reduce 90-day mortality by preventing metabolic and fluid complications of severe AKI.

methods.design: Multicentre, international, pragmatic, randomised, allocation-concealed, open-label superiority trial.

inclusion: Severe AKI defined as KDIGO stage 2 or 3
Clinician declaration of equipoise regarding KRT timing
exclusion: Urgent indications for KRT (severe electrolyte/acid-base disturbance, fluid overload compromising oxygenation)
Scenarios where KRT timing was non-discretionary (imminent need, competing priorities, specific contraindications)

methods.intervention: Accelerated strategy: initiate KRT ASAP and within 12 hours of eligibility. Modality, prescription, and anticoagulation were pragmatic (68.4% initial CRRT). Median time from randomisation to KRT was 1.6 hours (IQR 0.9–2.8); time from eligibility to KRT was 6.0 hours (IQR 4.0–8.8).
methods.comparison: Standard strategy: KRT discouraged unless conventional indications developed or AKI persisted. 61.8% received KRT. Median time from randomisation to KRT was 25.6 hours (IQR 18.7–47.1); time from eligibility to KRT was 31.8 hours (IQR 18.9–71.8).
methods.blinding: Open-label (unblinded delivery); primary mortality outcome is objective.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned n=2,866 to detect a 15% relative (6% absolute) reduction in 90-day mortality from 40% control mortality with 90% power (alpha=0.05). 3,019 randomised; 2,927 included in modified ITT primary analysis.
secondary_outcomes: Receipt of KRT during index admission
Composite of death or KRT dependence at 90 days
KRT dependence at 90 days among survivors
Major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at 90 days
ICU length of stay among survivors
Adverse events and serious adverse events

headline_bullets: 90-day all-cause mortality was essentially identical between accelerated and standard strategies (43.9% vs 43.7%).
38.2% of standard-strategy patients never required KRT during their admission.
Accelerated initiation increased KRT dependence among survivors at 90 days (10.4% vs 6.0%) and increased adverse events (23.0% vs 16.5%).

outcomes_table.note: No mortality benefit with accelerated initiation

outcomes_table.outcome: Received any KRT during index admission
outcomes_table.note: 38.2% of standard strategy patients avoided KRT

outcomes_table.outcome: Death or KRT dependence at 90 days
outcomes_table.note: Composite outcome did not show benefit
Worse renal recovery with accelerated strategy

outcomes_table.outcome: Major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at 90 days
ICU length of stay in survivors (median days, IQR)
outcomes_table.note: No significant ICU length of stay advantage
Higher rehospitalisation rate in accelerated group survivors
Significant increase in complications with accelerated strategy

subgroup_table.subgroup: Baseline KDIGO stage, sepsis, or surgical status

safety: Any adverse event: 23.0% (346/1503) accelerated vs 16.5% (245/1489) standard (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.21–1.62, P<0.001)
Serious adverse events: 1.0% (15/1503) accelerated vs 0.5% (8/1489) standard (P=0.15)

domains.notes: Central, web-based randomisation stratified by site using variable block sizes (2 and 4); allocation concealment maintained.
Open-label due to nature of intervention; primary mortality outcome is objective, though open-label design permits co-intervention discretion.
3,019 randomised; 2,927 analysed in modified ITT (3.0% excluded post-randomisation due to consent withdrawal or lost follow-up).
Strong separation in KRT exposure (96.8% vs 61.8%) and median time from eligibility to KRT (6.0 h vs 31.8 h).
Well balanced across groups (SAPS II 59.6 vs 59.5; SOFA 11.7 vs 11.9; mechanical ventilation 75.3% vs 78.5%; vasopressors 68.8% vs 72.0%; initial CRRT 68.4% vs 70.6%).

internal_validity.verdict: High internal validity with robust allocation, high protocol adherence, and substantial exposure separation.

domains.notes: Large, multinational cohort (168 ICUs across 15 countries) with severe AKI and high baseline acuity (~44% 90-day mortality).
Applies directly to ICU patients with severe AKI lacking immediate life-threatening indications; requires monitoring infrastructure to ensure safe delayed initiation.

external_validity.verdict: High generalisability to well-resourced ICUs managing severe AKI with close monitoring capacity.

strengths: Large sample size (n=3,019) across 168 ICUs in 15 countries
Pragmatic trial design reflecting real-world clinical practice
Substantial and distinct separation in timing and KRT exposure
Objective primary endpoint with low overall rate of post-randomisation loss
Careful adjudication of secondary kidney outcomes
limitations: Open-label design introduces potential co-intervention bias
Eligibility dependent on clinician-declared equipoise, introducing population heterogeneity
Secondary outcomes were not adjusted for multiple comparisons
Variable standard care monitoring and trigger criteria across participating sites

critical_appraisal.summary: STARRT-AKI is a definitive, high-quality pragmatic trial showing that routine early KRT initiation for severe AKI provides no survival advantage while increasing physical harms and dialysis dependence.
strengths: Rigorous allocation concealment and large multinational sample
Clear operational separation in KRT delivery and timing
Objective outcome measures with complete follow-up
weaknesses: Equipoise entry requirement may introduce selection bias
Lack of multiplicity correction for secondary endpoints

sections.authors_conclusion: In critically ill patients with severe AKI, an accelerated KRT strategy did not significantly lower 90-day all-cause mortality compared with a standard strategy, but led to more adverse events.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Practice-changing: Routine accelerated KRT initiation should not be performed for severe AKI alone without conventional urgent triggers.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with severe AKI (KDIGO stage 2/3) without emergent metabolic or fluid indications.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Do not delay KRT when life-threatening hyperkalemia, severe refractory acidosis, or severe fluid overload are present.
implementation_caveats: Watchful waiting requires continuous ICU monitoring to promptly rescue patients who develop urgent indications
38.2% of patients managed with watchful waiting avoid KRT entirely

controversies.notes: Requiring clinician-declared equipoise likely excluded patients at the extremes of immediate necessity or rapid recovery.
Higher 90-day KRT dependence in accelerated survivors (10.4% vs 6.0%) may stem from dialysis-induced hypotension and ischemic renal injury, particularly in patients with baseline CKD.

controversies.topic: Utility of KDIGO stage timing triggers
controversies.notes: Relying strictly on KDIGO AKI staging to trigger KRT is overly broad, as 38.2% of standard group patients recovered without KRT.
Correspondence noted rare hyperkalemia deaths in standard group and timing overlap between late-accelerated and early-standard patients.

context_related_trials.relation: Aligned with STARRT-AKI showing delayed KRT strategy avoids dialysis in many patients without increasing mortality.
Supported STARRT-AKI findings by showing early KRT initiation in septic shock AKI provides no survival benefit.
Single-center trial that previously suggested early KRT benefit; refuted by STARRT-AKI's pragmatic multinational design.

unresolved_questions: How to prospectively identify patients with non-recovering persistent AKI who benefit from earlier KRT
Safety and outcomes of watchful waiting in non-ICU or low-resource settings with less intensive monitoring

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Adopt monitored watchful waiting for severe ICU AKI without urgent indications to avoid unnecessary dialysis and reduce complications.
